items.title: How to Constrain AI to Do Its Job Well
items.summary: Generative AI is only a few years old, so making it predictable and reliable means experimenting with different prompts, workflows, and techniques. Providing detailed instructions, constrained outputs, and layers of automated review can keep AI’s outputs predictable and easy to check. We’re applying what we can learn from other researchers, and trying some new routes of our own, all within corrections.

items.title: A Bigger Bench: How Recidiviz is Partnering with Nonprofits to Scale Reentry Support
items.summary: Opportunities is now live across every state correctional facility in Arizona, through our partnership with Edovo—a digital learning platform that gives incarcerated people access to free educational, vocational, and personal development content. To date, over 29,000 individuals in Arizona have accessed the app. That statewide reach is what makes the partnerships with Inside Out Network (ION) and CEO possible, helping us connect people to new resources at exactly the right moment before release.

items.title: Part I: A mapping of tech in the criminal justice system
items.summary: This is the first part in a four-part series Recidiviz has written to summarize some of the biggest issues we see with the use of technology in the criminal justice space and to create a “playbook” with specific recommendations that practitioners can utilize in tech procurement, integration, and deployment. As always, we welcome thoughts and feedback.

items.title: Under the Hood: Why Our Platform Is Open Source, Modular, and Interoperable
items.summary: Every day, corrections software supports decisions with enormous stakes for public safety and people’s liberty. Too often, the agencies responsible for those decisions don't control the technology shaping them. We designed the Recidiviz Corrections Platform differently—an open source software that is modular and interoperable—because software funded with public money should be transparent and agencies should have autonomy and flexibility over their systems.

items.title: Part III: Tips for procuring and adopting criminal justice technology
items.summary: The criminal justice system is awash with new tech tools and inherently a difficult place to establish data-driven feedback loops. Practitioners looking to use technology must wade through a dizzying array of options to determine what to use, when to upgrade, and how to implement changes and track impact. Drawing on both what we’ve learned from building Recidiviz and successful practices from the private sector and government, we created this guide to help criminal justice practitioners procure and deploy technology effectively.

items.title: Part IV: Breaking Down Data Analytics and AI in Criminal Justice
items.summary: In recent years, artificial intelligence and data analytics have exploded in popularity. The criminal justice tech space is no exception: many new tools are AI-enabled, including algorithmic risk assessments, facial recognition, and gunshot detection. But these tools aren’t perfect. This posts walks through the differences between common types of tools, and provides practical, actionable advice to practitioners for use during the procurement and deployment process.

items.title: Beyond the Buzz: Reflections from Convening Leaders on Transforming Corrections with AI
items.summary: This post recaps an intimate convening of corrections, philanthropy, and tech leaders who gathered on the eve of the Recidiviz Partner Summit to explore how AI can move corrections beyond buzzwords toward real-world impact. items.title: Part II: Why good data and feedback loops are hard to come by
items.summary: Imagine you’ve just built and deployed a new software tool for consumers — say, better spell-check for email. Building and launching that tool is only half the battle — the big test is what happens after. How much time are users spending with the tool? How often does it crash, or do they seem to get stuck and walk away? How satisfied are they with the usability of the tool? What do they need that it can’t do yet (for instance, checking grammar)? And most importantly, to what extent is the tool actually impacting their goal: to send messages faster and with fewer mistakes? Based on the answers to these questions and more, your team will spend a lot of time on the next stage: iterating and making incremental changes, all the while ensuring that the quality of the product stays high throughout the process.
